title: "5 · Reproducing Open Mike — diminishing returns"
subtitle: "Does research output per dollar fall as a PI's grant support rises?"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: show
jupyter: python3
---

The NIH Extramural Nexus ("Open Mike", M. Lauer) repeatedly found **diminishing
returns** to grant support: as a principal investigator's total NIH funding
rises, research **output per dollar** falls ("Award or Reward?"; the Grant
Support Index work). This notebook reproduces that pattern from public data.

**Our approximation.** Support = total RePORTER funding per PI (a proxy for the
internal Grant Support Index). Output = summed iCite **Relative Citation Ratio
(RCR)** over the PI's authoritatively linked publications. See
`docs/open-mike-use-cases.md` for the full reproducibility catalog.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from nih_science_agent.tools import meta_research as meta
```

## Run the analysis over a bounded portfolio

We take a focused NIDDK portfolio so PIs span a real range of grant support, then
analyze a stratified sample across that range (publication fetching is the cost).

```{python}
res = meta.grant_support_vs_productivity(
    institutes=["NIDDK"], query="beta cell", fiscal_years=[2014, 2015],
    funding_floor=200_000, max_pis=48,
)
print(f"{res.pis_analyzed} of {res.pis_total} PIs analyzed")
for n in res.notes:
    print(" -", n)
```

## Output per dollar by funding quartile

```{python}
pd.DataFrame([b.model_dump() for b in res.bins])[
    ["label", "n_pis", "mean_funding", "mean_weighted_rcr", "mean_rcr_per_million"]
]
```

Output-per-dollar should decline across the lower quartiles — the diminishing-
returns signature. The Spearman correlation between support and output-per-dollar
is negative when the pattern holds:

```{python}
print("Spearman(support, output/$):", res.spearman_funding_vs_output_per_dollar)
```

## Support vs output (the sublinear curve)

The core claim is that *total* output rises with funding but **sublinearly** — so
a log-log slope below 1 indicates diminishing returns.

```{python}
df = pd.DataFrame([r.model_dump() for r in res.rows])
df = df[(df["total_funding"] > 0) & (df["weighted_rcr"] > 0)]
ax = df.plot.scatter(x="total_funding", y="weighted_rcr", loglog=True,
                     title="PI grant support vs summed RCR (log-log)")
ax.set_xlabel("total funding ($)"); ax.set_ylabel("summed RCR (output)")
```

## Honest reading

This bounded, single-topic sample (~48 PIs, two fiscal years) **directionally**
reproduces the pattern but is underpowered and noisy at the high-funding end —
unlike Lauer's analyses over tens of thousands of investigators. Faithful
population-scale reproduction needs the **ExPORTER bulk files in DuckDB**, not
on-demand API queries (the API caps offsets well below NIH's annual award count).
Other caveats baked into the tool's `notes`: output is lifetime RCR (recent
awards are right-censored) and authoritative-only (a floor), and support is a
funding proxy for the Grant Support Index.
